alternate_names: St. Joseph Church; German Catholic Church
address_historical: Northeast corner of Market and Hill Streets
structural_system: brick masonry
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Temporary post-fire frame St. Joseph's church; pre-fire church destroyed in 1871
postfire_code_context: Permanent brick rebuilding followed the parish's temporary post-fire frame structure.
notes: Cornerstone laid in October 1876; dedicated October 6, 1878; reported cost about $40,000.

address_historical: North Avenue crossing of the Chicago River
structural_system: combination swing bridge and turntable
postfire_code_context: Municipal movable-bridge construction supported the rebuilt city's river traffic and street network.
notes: Begun August 28, 1877 and completed in January 1878; 150 feet long, with 17-foot roadway, 4-foot sidewalk, 29-foot overall width, and $7,149 cost.

alternate_names: Fullerton Avenue bridge at north city limits
address_historical: Fullerton Avenue at the north city limits; joint City of Chicago-Town of Lake View crossing
owner_or_developer: City of Chicago and Town of Lake View
structural_system: pivot bridge
postfire_code_context: Joint-jurisdiction infrastructure extended the street network at Chicago's northern boundary.
notes: Contract awarded October 1, 1877; completed January 19, 1878; 125 feet long, 17.4-foot roadway, 20 feet overall. Andreas says Chicago's two-thirds cost was $2,970.50, wording that merits scan verification.

alternate_names: Eighteenth Street viaduct at Lumber Street
address_historical: Eighteenth Street at Lumber Street over the Pittsburgh, Fort Wayne & Chicago and Chicago, Alton & St. Louis railway tracks
owner_or_developer: City of Chicago; Pittsburgh, Fort Wayne & Chicago Railway Company contribution
structural_system: wrought-iron superstructure with two truss-girder spans
postfire_code_context: A permanent iron viaduct reduced street-rail conflicts in the rapidly rebuilding industrial city.
notes: Work began August 1 or 3, 1878; completed December 18, 1878; put in operation February 7, 1879. Andreas contains conflicting total and substructure costs ($20,409.16/$15,215.16 versus $17,196.56/$10,403.43); the wrought-iron superstructure is separately stated as $11,194.

address_historical: Lake Michigan shore at Lincoln Park
structural_system: Netherlands-plan brush mattresses laid in three to five feet of water
postfire_code_context: Permanent engineered shore protection replaced temporary expedients and shaped the lakefront land edge.
notes: Andreas states construction commenced in 1878 using the Netherlands plan. Completion date and surviving fabric require park-commission annual reports and georeferencing.

canonical_name: Chicago City Hall and Cook County Court House construction phase
alternate_names: City Hall and County Court House complex; fifth Chicago City Hall
address_historical: Original Court House Square; block bounded by Clark, Randolph, LaSalle, and Washington Streets
architect_or_builder: J. J. Egan (uniform exterior); L. D. Cleveland (city interior and construction supervision); Thomlinson & Reed (cut stone); John Angus (masonry); J. P. Sexton (iron)
owner_or_developer: City of Chicago and Cook County
structural_system: stone, brick, granite, and iron civic complex
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Court House and City Hall destroyed in 1871; temporary Rookery City Hall occupied 1872-1885
postfire_code_context: Permanent monumental masonry and iron construction on the original civic square embodied long-term post-fire institutional rebuilding.
notes: On April 17, 1878 the city awarded contracts of $477,693 for cut stone, $90,519 for masonry, and $105,302 for iron work. The joint complex was not ready for occupancy until January-February 1885.

canonical_name: U.S. Government Building and Post Office construction phase
alternate_names: Chicago Custom House and Post Office; U.S. Government Building
address_historical: Block bounded by Adams, Clark, Jackson, and Dearborn Streets
original_use: post office, custom house, sub-treasury, federal courts, pension and internal revenue offices
architect_or_builder: Alfred B. Mullett (original design); U.S. Treasury Supervising Architect's Office
structural_system: fireproof stone, iron, and brick
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Federal post office and custom house destroyed in the Great Chicago Fire
postfire_code_context: Explicitly fireproof federal construction replaced dispersed rented quarters described in 1878 as vulnerable to fire.
notes: The June 10, 1878 Congressional Record documents active work, a $300,000 bill appropriation plus $100,000 deficiency funding, and a proposed acceleration toward 1879 occupancy. The post office occupied part of the basement in April 1879; the entire building was completed about 1880.

canonical_name: First Regiment Illinois National Guard Armory I
address_historical: Jackson Street between Michigan and Wabash Avenues; later 22-26 Jackson Street
original_use: military drill, company rooms, exhibitions, concerts, and rifle practice
owner_or_developer: Union Mutual Life Insurance Company of Maine; leased to First Regiment Illinois National Guard
structural_system: rough-stone Gothic front; iron posts; timber roof; double floors with mortar sound-deadening
postfire_code_context: Purpose-built masonry and iron institutional construction reflected permanent civic investment after the 1877 labor riots.
notes: Contemporary report said completion was expected September 1, perhaps ten days later. Reported construction cost was $22,000 against an $18,000 limit, plus about $1,400 for the rear boiler and engine room.

address_historical: 83 S. Halsted Street, near Madison Street
owner_or_developer: William B. Clapp (owner); J. K. Emmett (lessee)
structural_system: brick side and rear walls; cut-stone three-story front
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Academy of Music I, destroyed by fire February 4-5, 1878
postfire_code_context: A rapid but substantially enlarged masonry reconstruction followed a theater fire within the post-fire city.
notes: Work was planned to begin in early May; the 75-by-120-foot, approximately $50,000 theater opened September 16, 1878. It burned October 12, 1880.

address_historical: 48-54 Dearborn Street
original_use: retail, classrooms, library, reading room, and gymnasium
structural_system: pressed brick with brownstone facings and trim
postfire_code_context: A purpose-built masonry educational and commercial block marked permanent cultural reconstruction.
notes: Erected for the Athenaeum's special accommodation; the institution moved in during spring 1878. Andreas gives a 90-by-80-foot plan and a two-story-height gymnasium occupying the upper floors; contemporary project citations place design/construction in 1877.

canonical_name: Chicago Fire Patrol Headquarters at 176 Monroe Street
address_historical: 176 Monroe Street
architect_or_builder: L. Z. Leiter (building erection); Chicago Fire Patrol members (interior finishing and arrangements)
owner_or_developer: L. Z. Leiter; Chicago Board of Underwriters/Chicago Fire Patrol
structural_system: masonry building; detailed material not stated
postfire_code_context: A permanent fire-salvage headquarters was a direct institutional response to Chicago's repeated conflagrations.
notes: Captain Bullwinkle's company formally opened and occupied the headquarters February 16, 1878. Andreas distinguishes Leiter's building work from the patrol members' interior finishing.

alternate_names: Servite Sisters convent and industrial home
address_historical: Corner of West Van Buren Street and Albany Avenue
original_use: convent, home, instruction, and vocational work
structural_system: brick and stone; iron entrance stairways
postfire_code_context: Substantial masonry institutional construction replaced the order's initial rented quarters at 1266 W. Van Buren.
notes: The sisters established their home in May 1878; construction on a 300-foot-square site began in 1878 and Vicar-General McMullen laid the cornerstone. Andreas still described the convent as unfinished in 1886; adjoining buildings were two and three stories.

canonical_name: House of the Good Shepherd North Wing
address_historical: Corner of North Market and Hill Streets
structural_system: masonry wing; exact material not stated
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: House of the Good Shepherd post-fire building erected 1872
postfire_code_context: A permanent institutional addition enlarged the rebuilt post-fire complex.
notes: A summer 1878 bazaar and benefits produced net receipts of $8,695, applied to erecting the north wing. The source does not state an exact completion date, so the annual placement records a materially documented construction expenditure/phase.

canonical_name: Church of the Immaculate Conception Priest's Residence
address_historical: Immediately south of the Church of the Immaculate Conception on the Near North Side
structural_system: likely brick masonry; exact material not stated
postfire_code_context: Parish residential construction supplemented the brick church rebuilt in 1874 around the surviving pre-fire basement.
notes: Andreas gives two conflicting costs—about $7,000 in the parish narrative and about $5,000 in Rev. P. T. Butler's biography. Precise historic street address remains unresolved.

canonical_name: Third Presbyterian Church on Ashland Avenue
address_historical: Ashland Avenue at or near Ogden Avenue
structural_system: masonry; exact material not stated
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Third Presbyterian Church at Washington and Carpenter Streets, sold in 1877
postfire_code_context: A large permanent West Side church replaced the congregation's earlier property after post-fire neighborhood movement.
notes: The new Ashland Avenue edifice was occupied in May 1878 and seated 1,900. It burned October 10, 1884 and was rebuilt materially on the old plan for reopening May 24, 1885.

canonical_name: Misses Grant's Seminary for Young Ladies
address_historical: 839 N. Dearborn Street / 27-31 W. Chestnut Street
address_modern: 839 N Dearborn St / 27-31 W Chestnut St
structural_system: red brick with gray limestone trim and brown ashlar ground level
postfire_code_context: A substantial masonry educational building represented permanent Near North Side rebuilding.
notes: The National Register nomination identifies the 1878 contributing building and describes its massive corner form, turret, gable, dormers, and contrasting masonry. Andreas notes that the school moved into its new building in November 1878.

address_historical: 827-833 N. Dearborn Street
structural_system: masonry; exact material not stated
postfire_code_context: A coordinated masonry rowhouse group contributed to permanent Near North Side residential reconstruction.
notes: The National Register nomination records four 1878 contributing rowhouses. Unit-level owners, exact completion dates, and later alterations need deed and permit research.

address_historical: Rear of 827-833 N. Dearborn Street
structural_system: masonry or frame not stated
postfire_code_context: Documented service buildings preserve the complete residential property system rather than only street-facing houses.
notes: The National Register nomination separately counts the 1878 barns as contributing buildings but does not attribute an architect in its resource table. Count and materials require inventory-sheet review.

alternate_names: J. M. W. Jones Printing Building; later Chicago Stock Exchange Building
address_historical: Northeast corner of Dearborn and Monroe Streets
original_use: heavy printing, paper company, and commercial tenants
owner_or_developer: Daniel F. Crilly; leased ground from Chicago Board of Education
structural_system: substantial heavy-load construction
postfire_code_context: Heavy-load commercial construction on a fire-cleared corner advanced the rebuilt printing district.
notes: Crilly leased the corner in 1878 and put up a five-story building for J. M. W. Jones Printing Company; Indianapolis Paper Company occupied the north part. Two stories were added in 1888. Later summaries that call it seven stories in 1878 conflate the phases.

alternate_names: Blakely & Brown Printing Building; Blakely, Brown & Marsh building
address_historical: 155-157 Dearborn Street; just north of the Chicago Journal office
owner_or_developer: B. R. Chambers; upper floors rented to Blakely & Brown
structural_system: masonry; exact material not stated
postfire_code_context: A five-story purpose-adapted commercial building supported the post-fire printing industry.
notes: The architect's project list identifies the 1878 Chambers block and its intended Blakely & Brown tenancy. Andreas independently says Blakely & Brown moved in 1878 to a five-story building they 'had erected' at 155-157 Dearborn; ownership/development wording needs lease research.

address_historical: Dearborn Avenue north of Schiller Street
structural_system: masonry or frame not stated
postfire_code_context: The project illustrates documented elite residential growth outside the central fire district.
notes: Listed among Cyrus P. Thomas's 1878 works with a contemporary Chicago Tribune citation; dimensions, material, exact address, and fate require the newspaper and permit record.

address_historical: Third Avenue at Taylor Street
structural_system: masonry or frame not stated
postfire_code_context: Purpose-built flats document the diversification and densification of post-fire housing.
notes: Listed among Cyrus P. Thomas's 1878 works with a May 19, 1878 Chicago Tribune citation. Exact unit count, dimensions, material, cost, and fate need the original notice and permit ledger.

canonical_name: Daniel Wells Commercial and Hotel Block
address_historical: Michigan Avenue at Harrison Street
original_use: stores, commercial space, and corner hotel
structural_system: masonry; exact material not stated
postfire_code_context: A substantial mixed-use block extended permanent masonry development along Michigan Avenue.
notes: The architect's project list dates the four-story block 1878-79 and cites Tribune notices of May 19, 1878 and April 6, 1879. The precise start and completion dates remain to be recovered from those notices.

canonical_name: Bemis & McAvoy Brewery East-Side Icehouse of 1878
address_historical: East side of South Park Avenue near Twenty-third Street
structural_system: substantial industrial construction; exact material not stated
postfire_code_context: Specialized industrial construction expanded a major post-fire brewery complex.
notes: Andreas states that two additional icehouses were erected on the east side of South Park Avenue in 1878 and 1879, implying one annual addition but not labeling the individual buildings. Entity matching to insurance maps is required.

address_historical: Bemis & McAvoy brewery complex near South Park Avenue and Twenty-third Street
original_use: brewery horses, vehicles, and service functions
structural_system: brick masonry
postfire_code_context: A permanent brick service building expanded the logistics capacity of a large brewery complex.
notes: Andreas explicitly dates the large brick barn to 1878. Its footprint, stories, architect, cost, and exact side of the avenue require Sanborn or Robinson map reconciliation.

alternate_names: New Adelphi Theater; later Haverly's Theater
address_historical: Northwest corner of Dearborn and Monroe Streets
structural_system: reused masonry walls with reconstructed interior and galleries
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: New Adelphi Theater opened January 11, 1875 in the old post-office walls
postfire_code_context: A major reconstruction reused strong surviving masonry while upgrading a prominent theater.
notes: Entirely reconstructed and redecorated in July-August 1878; reopened August 4. Work included plate glass, new scenery and curtain, frescoing, upholstery, and carpets, at a reported minimum cost of $8,500.

alternate_names: Foley's Billiard Hall; Hamlin Brothers garden and vaudeville; later Grand Opera House
address_historical: Rear of the Hamlin Brothers property on the former Bryan Hall and Hooley's Opera House site
owner_or_developer: "Hamlin Brothers; property passed to William C. Reynolds about 1878"
structural_system: reconstructed existing hall and adjoining fabric
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Foley's Billiard Hall, later garden and vaudeville theater
postfire_code_context: Repeated adaptive reuse converted post-fire commercial entertainment fabric into a regular theater.
notes: The former 1873 billiard hall/garden/vaudeville was reconstructed as a regular theater and opened in September 1878 as Hamlin's Theater. It was reconstructed again in 1880 as the Grand Opera House.

canonical_name: Fullerton Avenue Pile Bridge reported as rebuilt
address_historical: Fullerton Avenue
structural_system: reported 225-foot bridge with 20-foot roadway
postfire_code_context: The source preserves a bridge-rebuild claim, but entity resolution is necessary before treating it as a separate 1878 structure.
notes: Andreas says a Fullerton Avenue bridge was rebuilt in 1878 at 225 by 20 feet for $1,490. Those dimensions and cost exactly match a Fullerton pile bridge reported in the 1874-75 Board of Public Works year, while a separate 125-foot pivot bridge was completed January 19, 1878. This row preserves the conflict and must not be double-counted in resolved statistics.
